paraphrase: The existence of Brahman is known because it is the self of all: everyone is aware that he exists and never thinks 'I am not'; but because there are conflicting views about what the self is, inquiry is needed.

Knowledge of an existing thing depends on the thing itself (vastu-tantra), not on the person's choice (puruṣa-tantra) as action does; knowledge of Brahman therefore depends on the thing, and inference serves only in support of the Upaniṣadic texts.

Liberation is not something to be produced, reached, modified or purified by action; it is eternal bodilessness, the very nature of Brahman. Hence Brahman-knowledge is not subordinate to injunctions, and the Upaniṣads are authoritative in themselves for an existent reality, not merely as adjuncts to ritual.

Quoted verses: once the self as the existent Brahman is known, the secondary and false selves (son, body) being negated, how could there be anything to be done? The self is a knower only until the self to be sought is known; once known, it is free from knower-hood, evil and defects.
notes: Three verses introduced 'api cāhuḥ'; later commentators ascribe them to Sundarapāṇḍya (low confidence).

paraphrase: After commenting on the sūtras as though the 'one consisting of bliss' were Brahman, Śaṅkara argues that it is a sheath (kośa) and that the sūtras rather refer to 'Brahman, the tail, the support' (TU 2.5): the suffix -maya denotes modification, and the bliss-sheath has parts (joy, delight) and is not the highest.

Śūdras are not eligible for Vedic study, but those like Vidura and Dharmavyādha attained knowledge through tendencies from former lives; the fruit of knowledge cannot be denied to them, and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas may be taught to all four classes.

Of the three teachers' views, Kāśakṛtsna's — that the supreme Lord himself exists as the individual self — accords with scripture; the difference between jīva and Brahman is due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of name and form produced by ignorance.

Brahman is both the material cause (like clay for pots) and the efficient cause (like the potter), since scripture promises that by knowing it everything is known and gives the illustration of clay and its products; there is no other overseer.

The effect (the world) is non-different from its cause (Brahman), a mere name dependent on speech, as pots are clay; all worldly and Vedic dealings are valid until the knowledge of the self as Brahman, as dream dealings are until waking; the Lord's lordship, omniscience and omnipotence depend on the limiting adjuncts of name and form produced by ignorance.

The Lord creates without any purpose of his own, as a king at leisure plays or as breathing goes on by itself; and scripture's account of creation is concerned only with the empirical realm of name and form produced by ignorance, its aim being to teach that Brahman is the self.
The Lord is like rain (parjanya), the common cause of all plants, whose varieties depend on their own seeds: inequality among beings depends on their own merit and demerit.

Having refuted the realist, idealist and void doctrines, Śaṅkara says the Buddha, by teaching three mutually incompatible doctrines, showed either incoherence or hostility toward beings, and that the Buddhist teaching is to be disregarded by those who seek the good.

The Pāñcarātra's worship of Vāsudeva, its practices of approach, offering, study and meditation, and its devotion are not refuted; what is refuted is the doctrine that the individual self (Saṅkarṣaṇa) and the mind originate from Vāsudeva.
notes: Placed at the section 2.2.42–45; exact sūtra of this remark uncertain.

paraphrase: The jīva is to be understood as a reflection (ābhāsa) of the supreme self, like the sun reflected in water; as the trembling of one reflection does not affect others, the karma of one jīva does not pass to another.
Brahman appears as if sharing the defects and differences of its adjuncts, as the sun's reflection seems to increase, decrease and tremble with the water; in itself it is untouched.

'Not so, not so' negates the two forms (gross and subtle, formed and formless) of Brahman already mentioned, not Brahman itself, which the text then names 'the reality of the real'; negation must end in something not negated.

Works such as sacrifice are needed not for the fruit of knowledge (liberation) but for the arising of knowledge, as a horse is used for drawing a chariot, not for ploughing; once knowledge has arisen they are not needed for liberation.

Repetition of the teaching is for one who does not realize at the first hearing; for one who understands 'tat tvam asi' at once, repetition is useless. Repetition removes the obstacles of doubt and contrary notions.
The knower of Brahman is untouched by future sins and his past sins are destroyed, because he realizes himself as the non-agent Brahman; this is the state of liberation while living.

Works that have already begun their effect (prārabdha) are not destroyed by knowledge but continue until exhausted, just as a potter's wheel keeps turning for a while after the push that set it going has ceased; for one who has knowledge, the body continues till death.
notes: The potter's-wheel illustration is placed here from memory (moderate confidence); a released arrow is used in the same sense elsewhere in the tradition.

paraphrase: The prāṇas of the knower of the attributeless Brahman do not depart: being Brahman, he merges here; the path of the gods is for those who meditated on the qualified Brahman.

Those who meditated on the qualified Brahman go by the path of light to the Brahma-world and are liberated with Hiraṇyagarbha at the end of the cycle (gradual liberation, krama-mukti); the knower of the attributeless Brahman is liberated at once.

The text's 'desiring this world (the self) alone, renunciants wander forth' enjoins renunciation; sacrifice, gifts and austerity produce the desire to know (vividiṣā), and the knower renounces all works.
The double negation 'not so, not so' excludes every specification by adjuncts; Brahman cannot be described by name, form, action, distinction, genus or quality, and is indicated only by negation.

Against the view that knowledge must be combined with works and that the world is really both one and many (difference-in-identity), Śaṅkara argues that difference and non-difference cannot both be real of one thing.
notes: Bhartṛprapañca's views are refuted at several places in the commentary (the opponent is named by Ānandagiri); the specific locator 5.1.1 (pūrṇam adaḥ) is given with low confidence.

paraphrase: 'Satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma' is a definition (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman's own nature: each word excludes what is opposed to it (the unreal, the insentient, the finite), and together they indicate Brahman without making it an object with attributes.

The five sheaths are taught progressively, each inner one presented as the self of the outer, so that the seeker is led from the food-sheath to Brahman, the support ('tail') of the bliss-sheath, which is not itself a sheath.
The word upaniṣad means the knowledge of Brahman, because for those who approach it with dispassion it loosens and destroys the seeds of saṃsāra such as ignorance, and leads them to Brahman.

Even one learned in scripture should not seek knowledge of Brahman independently; he should approach, with fuel in hand, a teacher who is learned in scripture (śrotriya) and established in Brahman (brahmaniṣṭha), who then teaches the calm, qualified disciple.

Verse 1 teaches the knower's renunciation of all desire and possession, covering the world with the Lord (the self); verse 2 ('performing works here one should wish to live a hundred years') is for those unable to take up knowledge, for whom works without attachment are the path.

Knowledge does not immediately end the body: 'for him the delay lasts only as long as he is not released (from the body); then he is merged' — the karma that has begun to bear fruit continues, like an arrow already released, until it is spent.
notes: The released-arrow image and its placement here are recalled with low confidence.

paraphrase: The Vedic dharma is twofold: that characterized by activity (pravṛtti), which leads to prosperity and higher worlds, and that characterized by withdrawal (nivṛtti), which leads to liberation; the Gītā teaches both, and its special aim is the supreme good through knowledge of the self preceded by renunciation.

Introducing the teaching, Śaṅkara argues at length that knowledge of the self cannot be combined with works as joint cause of liberation, since knowledge (the self is actionless) and works (which require the sense of agency) have opposite presuppositions.

One who sees inaction in action sees that the self is actionless and that action belongs to body and senses; one who sees action in inaction sees that inactivity too, when claimed as one's own, is an act — such a one is wise.
Of the four kinds of devotees, the knower (jñānī), ever united and devoted to the One, is the best; the Lord is dear to him and he to the Lord, since the knower is the Lord's very self.

The Lord is the knower of the field in all fields; the appearance of the embodied one as a transmigrating agent-enjoyer is due to ignorance, which is itself not the self's attribute but belongs to the field (the instrument).

'Abandoning all dharmas' means renouncing all works, together with the notion of agency; taking refuge in the Lord alone means knowing oneself as the one Lord; knowledge alone, not works or their combination, is the means to the highest good.

The knowledge of Brahman, the means to liberation, is to be taught repeatedly until firmly grasped, to a disciple who is calm, self-controlled, free from faults, obedient, devoted to the teacher, and longing for liberation, who has approached in the proper way.

The teacher is one able to argue and to answer, retentive, calm, self-controlled, compassionate, learned in scripture, unattached to enjoyments, having renounced all works, a knower of Brahman established in Brahman, free of pretence and pride, whose sole aim is to help others.

A model dialogue: the disciple, asked who he is, answers with his birth and caste; the teacher shows that body, caste and rites belong to the not-self, and leads him to know himself as eternal, pure awareness in which the cognitions of the intellect appear and which is never itself an object.

Parisaṃkhyāna, for seekers who wish to destroy merit and demerit and to avoid new ones: one reflects that sound and the other objects are not-self, change and depart, while 'I' am of the nature of pure awareness, unconnected, changeless, not an object — thus detaching from them.

In the chapter on 'tat tvam asi', Śaṅkara holds that once the meaning of the sentence is understood, the self is known as free from suffering; he rejects the view that one must further practise repeated meditation (prasaṅkhyāna) on the sentence for knowledge to become effective.

paraphrase: Meditation on the attributeless Brahman, though an act of mind, leads to liberating knowledge, as mistaking the light of a gem for the gem leads one to the gem (a 'consistent error', saṃvādi-bhrama); inquiry is best, but those unable to inquire should meditate.

paraphrase: Renunciation is twofold: that of the seeker who desires to know (vividiṣā-sannyāsa), a means to knowledge, and that of the knower (vidvat-sannyāsa), a means to liberation while living.

Knowledge of the truth, destruction of latent tendencies (vāsanā-kṣaya) and dissolution of the mind (mano-nāśa) are to be practised together, each supporting the others; without the latter two, knowledge does not bring the stable freedom of the jīvanmukta.
The purposes of liberation while living are five: protection of knowledge, austerity, absence of conflict, cessation of suffering, and the manifestation of bliss.

The knower is graded by the seven stages of knowledge (from the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha): one at the fourth is a knower of Brahman; at the fifth, sixth and seventh, increasingly excellent knowers, distinguished by how far they rise from absorption by themselves or by others.

paraphrase: The world is false (mithyā) because it is seen, insentient and limited, like the silver seen in shell; falsity is defended under five definitions: not being the locus of either existence or non-existence (Pañcapādikā); being the counterpositive of the absence in all three times in the very locus of appearance (Vivaraṇa); being removable by knowledge (Vivaraṇa); being the counterpositive of an absolute absence in its own locus (Citsukha); being other than the real (Ānandabodha).

A graded series of mistaken views of the self: the most ignorant take the son as the self, Cārvākas the gross body, the senses, the vital breath or the mind; a Buddhist the intellect; Prābhākaras and Naiyāyikas the self as associated with ignorance; Bhāṭṭas consciousness mixed with ignorance; another Buddhist the void — each refuted by the next and all by scripture and experience.

In 'tat tvam asi' the relation of the words is co-reference, of their meanings qualifier–qualified, and of the self to them indicated–indicator; since the direct meanings conflict, exclusive implication and non-exclusive implication both fail, and exclusive-non-exclusive implication (bhāga-lakṣaṇā) applies, as in 'this is that Devadatta': dropping the contradictory parts, pure consciousness is indicated.

On hearing the mahāvākya, a mental mode in the form of the partless Brahman (akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti) arises; it pervades Brahman and destroys ignorance, but the reflected consciousness in it does not illumine Brahman, which is self-luminous — as a lamp is not needed to see the sun.

Hearing is the determination, by the six marks, that the Upaniṣads' purport is the non-dual Brahman: opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise and demonstration; reflection is the continual consideration of this by reasoning in accord with it; contemplation is the flow of like ideas excluding unlike ones.

Samādhi is twofold: with distinctions (savikalpa), in which the mental mode takes the form of Brahman while the distinction of knower and known remains, like a clay elephant seen as clay; and without distinctions (nirvikalpa), in which that distinction dissolves, like salt dissolved in water. Its eight auxiliaries are restraint, observance, posture, breath control, withdrawal, holding, meditation and (savikalpa) samādhi.

Nirvikalpa samādhi has four obstacles: dullness (laya), the mind's lapse into sleep; distraction (vikṣepa), its turning to other things; latent attachment (kaṣāya), its stiffening by impressions of attachment; and relishing (rasāsvāda), its enjoyment of the bliss of savikalpa samādhi.

The one liberated while living, knowing Brahman, lives with the body sustained by prārabdha; his conduct continues in good tendencies only, without sense of agency; the virtues of humility and the like remain as ornaments (quoting Naiṣkarmyasiddhi 4.62 and 4.69); at death his prāṇas merge and he abides as Brahman.

Verbal testimony gives knowledge through expectancy, compatibility, proximity and intended purport; the Veda is not composed by a person but reproduced by Īśvara at each creation in the same order as before.

Brahman has a defining mark of its own nature (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa: existence, consciousness, bliss) and an incidental mark (taṭastha-lakṣaṇa: being the cause of the world's origin, sustenance and dissolution), as a house is pointed out by the crow sitting on it.

Dissolution (pralaya) is fourfold: daily (deep sleep), occasional (at the end of Brahmā's day), elemental (of all effects into prakṛti at the end of Brahmā's life) and final (ātyantika, liberation through knowledge).

Liberation is the attainment of bliss and the removal of sorrow, which is Brahman itself; its means is the knowledge of Brahman, arising from hearing and the rest in one endowed with the four means; worship of the qualified Brahman leads to the Brahma-world and gradual liberation.
